After a week of trying many models for fiction writing, Gemma 4 26B A4B IT (Heretic) is the first one which feels actually capable.
In the very early days I was able to finetune a gen 1 llama base model on my own writing, but I wanted to avoid setting that all up again and was hoping that I could instruct a more modern model into writing what I want.
However every model which could fit on my GPU which I tried was a disappointment, even though they were widely praised as the best. Short contexts, frequent incoherency, not grasping the prompt, not grasping the subtleties of example text snippets, etc.
I was about to give up, but decided whatever I'll try an 'unlocked' version of the new Gemma models even though I expected that it would be bad due to the original training dataset being overly focused on math and 'safe' corporate content. And holy hell, I finally found a model which just works, and works incredibly well. There's a chance it might have included some of my own writing in some capacity which is out there across the web going back a few decades, since it locks right onto my style, themes, settings, etc. However when I query it for any specifics it doesn't seem to know them, so I don't think that's the case.
I suspect that I'll be renting some cloud processing for the first time ever to finetune this soon and make it even better. But even out of the box it's extremely capable. If anybody is looking for a strong local writing model, Gemma 4 is amazing. I used the following recommended creative writing settings, where I could find equivalents in LM Studio.

Mixtral: A Promising Model with Unforeseen Challenges
I was able to spend significant time yesterday testing Mistral in a plethora of ways. If you go into it with high hopes off the bat, you are going to be disappointed. Just putting that out there upfront. There are bugs with this model. Why are those bugs there though, and are they fixable? Possibly, possibly not. This is the first time a model of this size with this architecture has been released for pure testing purposes. I do not know.
One of the most concerning issues is the model's apparent "AI Multiple Personality Disorder." This phenomenon manifests as inconsistencies in the responses generated by different component models, leading to incoherent and unreliable outputs. This inconsistency is particularly pronounced when the model is presented with challenging questions, where it often performs worse than other LLM models.
While the exact cause of this inconsistency remains unclear, it's likely to be linked to several factors. The training data used for Mixtral may not have adequately addressed such scenarios, leading the models to be unprepared for them. Additionally, the controller, responsible for selecting the appropriate model for each query, may not be sophisticated enough to consistently make optimal decisions.
Furthermore, I do not know how the developer's setup the model's encoder/decoder configuration, which hinders a deeper understanding of its behavior. As an experienced MoE developer, I can attest that even minor changes in this configuration can have drastic effects on the model's performance. Without this information, it's impossible to definitively assess Mixtral's potential and potential pathways for improvement.
Despite these challenges, Mixtral's release marks a significant milestone in the development of MoE-based LLMs. It provides invaluable data and insights that can guide future research and development efforts. It's crucial to remember that Mixtral is still in its early stages of development and should be treated as a test model. More research is needed to fully understand its capabilities and limitations, optimize its performance, and ensure its reliability and consistency.
Bottom line, I am writing this because I am afraid people are going to use the model, think it is utter trash, and move on, while trashing it. As someone who has actually played around with MoE's pretty extensively, I have solved problems that Mixtral is currently displaying by adding literally one line of code to the encoder/decoder.
Is that all Mixtral needs? I do not know; I do not possess a personal server to test these things on that level to where I can actually play around with the backend of this model and stand it up. It is going to take time to do research with this model. MoE's are weird. You have to fine tune every single aspect of them. These things will take time to research out. Please, just don't trash the overall architecture as a knee jerk reaction. More testing is needed.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next vs Opus 5.5: Six-way benchmark on a real Rust feature with Claude Code and Pi
Reposting again since original post got removed by Reddit for some reason (I have no idea why)

A few of you pointed out in my last post that comparing Flash-Next and Opus with different harnesses and effort levels wasn't fair. So here is a more controlled comparison.

Same task for every run: a real feature from the LlamaStash roadmap (save llama-server's KV cache before an unload and restore it when the model comes back). Six combinations, each run twice, so 12 PRs. Flash-Next ran locally on my Strix Halo laptop (Flow Z13) via Halogen (~Q4 quant). Opus 5.5, Flash-Next, and Kimi K3 scored every PR on seven review questions plus CI.

Combination	Score (of 8)	Time	API cost	Tokens (in / cached / out)
Claude Code + Opus 5.5, xhigh	6.94 (87%)	43.5 min	$17.78	507k / 48.3M / 203k
Claude Code + Opus 5.5, medium	6.25 (78%)	23.4 min	$6.52	242k / 13.4M / 95k
Claude Code + Flash-Next, medium	5.5 (69%)	45.3 min	$0.32	445k / 13.5M / 82k
Pi + Flash-Next, xhigh	5.44 (68%)	63.8 min	$0.67	316k / 35.0M / 134k
Claude Code + Flash-Next, xhigh	5.38 (67%)	49.5 min	$0.39	269k / 18.9M / 99k
Pi + Flash-Next, medium	5.06 (63%)	48.1 min	$0.56	242k / 29.1M / 117k
Scores are the average of both runs. Time, cost and tokens are from the second run, where the 100k-token benchmark numbers were given in the prompt. Flash-Next cost is at the QwenCloud price for Qwen3.8-Flash; I ran it locally, so it cost me only electricity.

TL;DR

All 12 runs finished and all 12 PRs pass the end-to-end test.

Opus wrote better code, 82% on average against 68% for Claude Code + Flash-Next and 66% for Pi + Flash-Next. The difference is in edge cases, tests and docs. The core feature works fine. The gap between Opus and Qwen is not that wide.

Flash-Next took 1.1x to 2.1x as long as Opus at the same effort.

With Flash-Next, Claude Code and Pi scored the same on the review questions. CI passed on 4 of 4 Claude Code PRs and 1 of 4 Pi PRs.

xhigh helped Opus a bit at 2.7x the cost. For Flash-Next, medium and xhigh scored about the same, and medium was faster in all 4 pairs.

Opus is still ahead, but Flash-Next was right behind, on my laptop, for the cost of electricity.

Also note that the models are not on the same league. Opus is a frontier model run at FP16 or atleast FP8. I ran Flash-Next on my laptop at 4.16 bpw. Flash-Next at FP8 should show a bit more quality.

The machine running Flash-Next ran at 70W TDP ceiling for the entire duration. I could have run it at 90W for slightly better speed but the fan noise and thermal stress was not worth it.

Full write-up with the detailed methodology and the per-run results and what each model missed: https://deepu.tech/qwen3.8-flash-next-vs-claude-opus-showdown

All 12 PRs are public if you want to read the code: https://github.com/deepu105/llamastash-b4r2/pulls

AI labs report benchmark scores 6.4% higher than independent testers, on average
I've been building [whatmodel.sh](http://whatmodel.sh/), an open source AI leaderboard, and wanted to see how a labs' own benchmark scores compare with independent testers.
Using 1,629 published benchmark results, I matched 611 comparisons of 180 models on 103 benchmarks. AI labs reported scores 6.4% higher on average for the same models on the same tests.
Everything is open: the dataset is CC BY-SA 4.0 and the code is MIT. Sources and their licenses are recorded, with links on each model's page.
Interactive chart: https://whatmodel.sh/claims
Data and code: https://github.com/jakemanger/whatmodel
